name: Mohs hardness
question: Which scratches which? 1 is soft as talc, 10 is diamond.

items.name: Talc
items.fact: Talc is the softest mineral on the scale and the main ingredient of talcum powder.

items.name: Gypsum
items.fact: Gypsum is the mineral in plaster and drywall.

items.name: Calcite
items.fact: Calcite makes up limestone and marble.

items.name: Fluorite
items.fact: Fluorite gave its name to fluorescence: many samples glow under UV light.

items.name: Apatite
items.fact: The enamel on your teeth is mostly a form of apatite.

items.name: Orthoclase feldspar
items.fact: Feldspars are the most common group of minerals in Earth's crust.

items.name: Quartz
items.fact: Quartz is hard enough to scratch window glass.

items.name: Topaz
items.fact: Pure topaz is colorless; most blue topaz in shops has been treated.

items.name: Corundum (ruby, sapphire)
items.fact: Ruby and sapphire are the same mineral, corundum, colored by different traces of metal.

items.name: Diamond
items.fact: One step above corundum, but about four times as hard.

items.name: Potassium metal
items.fact: Potassium is soft enough to cut with a butter knife.

items.name: Lead
items.fact: Lead is soft enough to mark paper, which is why 'lead' pencils got their name (they're actually graphite).

items.name: Zinc
items.fact: Most modern 'copper' pennies in the US are mostly zinc inside.

items.name: Brass
items.fact: Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc.

items.name: Iron
items.fact: Pure iron is surprisingly soft; carbon turns it into much harder steel.

items.name: Glass
items.fact: A steel knife and window glass are close in hardness.

items.name: Silicon
items.fact: Silicon wafers for computer chips are cut from huge single crystals.

items.name: Tungsten
items.fact: Tungsten has the highest melting point of any metal.

items.name: Chromium
items.fact: Chromium is the hardest pure metal, which is why it's used for plating.

items.name: Sapphire
items.fact: Synthetic sapphire is used for scratch-resistant watch faces.
